VBO:0200667.summary: The Hellenic Hound is a Greek scent hound built to follow a trail over broken terrain. Its lean, muscular outline, hanging ears and short black-and-tan coat form a distinct working silhouette, with stamina and a resonant voice suited to rough mountain ground.
VBO:0200667.interestingFact: Its standard places it among medium-sized scent hounds with a working trial.
VBO:0200667.historicalRoots: Greek scent hound traditionally worked over varied, rocky terrain.

VBO:0200668.summary: Hertha Pointer is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200669.summary: Hierran Wolfdog is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200670.summary: The Himalayan Sheepdog is better understood as a regional livestock-guardian population than as one perfectly uniform show-ring breed. Across Himalayan communities, large mountain dogs have worked around flocks, homes, and difficult terrain for generations. Coat, size, and local names vary between regional populations.
VBO:0200670.interestingFact: “Himalayan Sheepdog” can cover related regional dogs with different local names and appearances—exactly the kind of diversity a global catalog should preserve instead of flattening.

VBO:0200671.summary: The Hokkaido is a sturdy Japanese hunting spitz associated with the island's Ainu people and its snowy climate. A harsh double coat, pricked ears and curled or sickle tail frame a compact, strong dog historically used on bear and other game.
VBO:0200671.interestingFact: It was designated a Japanese natural monument in 1937, when the regional name Hokkaido became official.
VBO:0200671.historicalRoots: Hokkaido hunting dog associated with Ainu communities.

VBO:0200673.summary: Hound is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200674.summary: Hovawart is a German estate guardian whose name joins old words for farmyard and watcher. Breeders rebuilt the type from farm dogs beginning in 1922, using other large working breeds to stabilize it. The result is a powerful, slightly long-bodied dog with a flowing coat and a more athletic outline than its size first suggests.
VBO:0200674.interestingFact: The revival program used, among others, German Shepherd Dogs, Newfoundlands, and Leonbergers.
VBO:0200674.historicalRoots: German farm and estate guardian rebuilt in the twentieth century.

VBO:0200678.summary: The Hungarian Greyhound, or Magyar Agár, is a robust sighthound tied to hunting traditions in Hungary. More substantial than many racing silhouettes, it combines a deep chest and strong legs with the speed for coursing; nineteenth-century crossings sought still greater pace.
VBO:0200678.interestingFact: The FCI history links the type to the Magyar settlement of Hungary and records later sighthound crosses.
VBO:0200678.historicalRoots: Hungarian hunting sighthound with medieval roots and nineteenth-century refinement.

VBO:0200679.summary: Transylvanian Hound is a dog breed or regional type associated with Hungary.

VBO:0200681.summary: Hungarian Smooth-Haired Vizsla is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200683.summary: The Huntaway is a New Zealand farm dog selected for its voice as much as its legs. Broadly built and variable in coat, it uses a deep bark to push sheep through yards and across steep pasture, announcing its position across the hills.
VBO:0200683.interestingFact: On a working farm, a huntaway's bark is an instruction to stock and a way for the handler to follow the dog's position.
VBO:0200683.historicalRoots: New Zealand voiced sheep-driving working dog.

VBO:0200684.summary: Huskamute is a named crossbreed. Dogs of this cross can vary widely in appearance and size, including within the same litter.

VBO:0200687.summary: Hygenhund is a dog breed or regional type associated with Norway.

VBO:0200688.summary: Ibizan Hound comes from Spain’s Balearic Islands, where hunters used it chiefly for rabbits in rocky, brushy terrain. Its tall, narrow frame, immense upright ears, and light-footed movement form a striking Mediterranean outline. Scent and hearing help it find rabbits even in dense cover.
VBO:0200688.interestingFact: When one Ibizan Hound finds a rabbit, others may join it in a coordinated hunt.

VBO:0200690.summary: Ibizan Podenco, Rough-Haired is a variety of Ibizan Hound.

VBO:0200691.summary: Ibizan Podenco, Smooth-Haired is a variety of Ibizan Hound.

VBO:0200692.summary: The Icelandic Sheepdog descends from dogs brought by Iceland’s Viking settlers and became essential to farm stock work. This lively spitz has upright ears, a curled tail and a thick coat suited to wind and weather, with a working style shaped by Icelandic terrain.
VBO:0200692.interestingFact: The FCI dates the settlers’ arrival to roughly AD 870–930.
VBO:0200692.historicalRoots: Icelandic farm and livestock dog descending from settler dogs.

VBO:0200693.summary: Ilio is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200695.summary: The Indian Pariah Dog, often called INDog, is an indigenous village-dog landrace of the Indian subcontinent. A moderate frame, upright ears, short coat and curved tail recur across rural populations whose local histories and colors vary.
VBO:0200695.interestingFact: The INDog Project distinguishes the indigenous type from the much broader category of all street dogs.

VBO:0200696.summary: Indian Spitz is a spitz-family companion dog kept in India and shown under its own name at native-breed events. The breed occupies a familiar place in Indian households as well as the country’s organized dog-show world.

VBO:0200697.summary: Inuit Dog is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200700.summary: Irish Red and White Setter is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200702.summary: The Irish Setter began as a red working bird dog, selected in Ireland for hunting game with stamina and style. A lean head, flowing chestnut coat and feathered tail give the breed its famous sweep, but its history is firmly rooted in field work.
VBO:0200702.interestingFact: The Irish Red Setter Club issued a breed standard in 1886 and has long paired shows with field trials.
VBO:0200702.historicalRoots: Irish red setter developed for bird hunting.

VBO:0200703.summary: Irish Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200704.summary: Irish Terrier is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200705.summary: The Irish Water Spaniel is a tall, tightly curled waterfowl dog with a smooth face and a startlingly bare-looking 'rat tail.' It has long worked in marsh and heavy cover, hunting and retrieving for wildfowlers; the dense liver curls protect the body while the tail keeps its own distinctive shape.
VBO:0200705.interestingFact: Its nearly naked tapering tail is so unusual that it has long been used as a clue in discussions of the breed's ancestry.

VBO:0200706.summary: Irish Wolfhound is the tallest of the sighthounds: a rough-coated, powerfully made dog that still moves with long-legged grace. In Ireland it historically pursued wolves, deer, and wild boar, with wolf hunting continuing into the seventeenth century. Great scale and an active coursing build appear together.
VBO:0200706.interestingFact: One of the earliest written accounts of Irish wolfhounds dates to 391 CE.

VBO:0200708.summary: Istrian Sheepdog is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200709.summary: The Istrian Short-Haired Hound is a white-and-orange scent hound of Croatia’s Adriatic region, traditionally used for hare and fox. Its clean, short coat and fine, strong frame give an agile outline; regional art and written records document hound types there for centuries.
VBO:0200709.interestingFact: A fourteenth-century Dubrovnik monastery carving is among the early records cited in its standard.
VBO:0200709.historicalRoots: Croatian Adriatic hare and fox scent hound.

VBO:0200710.summary: The Istrian Wire-Haired Hound is a Croatian scent hound whose coarse white coat and orange markings suit the cold, stony hills of the eastern Adriatic. It follows hare, fox and boar with stamina; the beard and rough texture set it apart from its smoother Istrian relative.
VBO:0200710.interestingFact: A 1719 manuscript describes the wire-haired Istrian hound, and says its breeding was already established earlier.

VBO:0200711.summary: Italian Bulldog is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200712.summary: Italian Cane Corso is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200713.summary: Italian Greyhound is a small sighthound with a square, delicately made body, fine skin, and the long-legged proportions of a much larger coursing dog. Small hounds of this kind traveled through the Mediterranean into Italy, where the type flourished in Renaissance courts. Its slender limbs retain a running dog’s silhouette.
VBO:0200713.interestingFact: Renaissance paintings frequently placed these small sighthounds beside nobles.
VBO:0200713.historicalRoots: Small Mediterranean sighthound developed in Italy.

VBO:0200716.summary: Italian Rough-Haired Segugio is a variety of Segugio Italiano associated with Italy.

VBO:0200717.summary: Italian Setter is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200721.summary: The Italian Spinone is a rugged Italian pointing dog with a wiry coat, heavy brows and a memorable beard. Its broad, steady trot and patient field style suit rough cover; references to similar rough-haired Italian dogs appear in old hunting writing and art.
VBO:0200721.interestingFact: The FCI cites a fifteenth-century Mantua fresco among depictions of the breed’s ancestors.
VBO:0200721.historicalRoots: Italian rough-haired pointing dog with longstanding field use.

VBO:0200724.summary: The Jack Russell Terrier began with Reverend John Russell's English fox-hunting dogs and was further developed in Australia. The small, flexible body is a little longer than tall, suited to going to ground; smooth, broken and rough coats all belong to the same working-terrier design.
VBO:0200724.interestingFact: The taller square Parson Russell and the shorter, longer-bodied Jack Russell took separate paths from related working stock.
VBO:0200724.historicalRoots: English fox-terrier line developed further in Australia.

VBO:0200731.summary: Jackshund is a named crossbreed. Dogs of this cross can vary widely in appearance and size, including within the same litter.

VBO:0200732.summary: Jagdterrier is a compact German hunting terrier created after the First World War by breeders focused on field performance. Its dark, wiry or smooth coat and small, sturdy body suit work below ground as well as flushing above it. The breed has remained associated with a wide range of demanding hunting tasks.
VBO:0200732.interestingFact: The foundation program deliberately selected black-and-tan terriers for underground hunting.

VBO:0200733.summary: The Jämthund is a large Swedish hunting spitz, long present in the north but recognized separately only in 1946. Its gray coat, erect ears and strong curled tail frame a dog used chiefly to find and bay elk, with endurance for lengthy work in forest country.
VBO:0200733.interestingFact: It was once judged together with the smaller Norwegian Elkhound before separate recognition.

VBO:0200734.summary: Japanese Akitainu is a variety of Akita associated with Japan and United States.

VBO:0200735.summary: The Japanese Chin is a tiny, fine-boned companion with a broad face, large dark eyes and a silky coat that falls in a mane-like ruff. Its upright carriage and plumed tail make a distinctly courtly silhouette; the breed's history belongs to East Asian palace companionship rather than field work.
VBO:0200735.historicalRoots: East Asian court companion developed in Japan.

VBO:0200736.summary: Japanese Pointer is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200737.summary: Japanese Retriever is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200740.summary: Japanese Spitz is a Japanese companion spitz with a pure-white standing coat, pointed muzzle, erect ears, and a plumed tail arched over the back. The breed emerged in the early twentieth century from white spitz dogs imported through several countries. Its small, well-balanced frame creates a crisp outline without the mass of a northern sledge dog.
VBO:0200740.interestingFact: A white German Spitz imported via Siberia and northeast China was exhibited in Tokyo in 1921.
VBO:0200740.historicalRoots: Japanese white-spitz companion developed in the twentieth century.

VBO:0200741.summary: The Japanese Terrier is a small, smooth-coated dog developed from imported fox terriers and local small dogs in Japan’s port cities. Its dark head and mostly white body make a crisp silhouette; it served mainly as a lapdog in Kobe and Yokohama before organized breeding fixed the type.
VBO:0200741.interestingFact: The FCI traces imported smooth fox terriers to Nagasaki trade with the Netherlands in the seventeenth century.
VBO:0200741.historicalRoots: Japanese port-city companion terrier refined in the early twentieth century.

VBO:0200743.summary: Japanese Tosa Inu is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200744.summary: The Jindo is a medium Korean spitz from Jindo Island, clean-lined and athletic with a curled or sickle tail and alert triangular ears. Its island history helped preserve a recognizable local type.
VBO:0200744.interestingFact: Korea protects the Jindo as a Natural Monument, tying the breed’s identity to Jindo Island as well as to its physical standard.
VBO:0200744.historicalRoots: Korean island spitz associated with Jindo County.

VBO:0200745.summary: Jonangi is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200746.summary: Jug is a named crossbreed. Dogs of this cross can vary widely in appearance and size, including within the same litter.

VBO:0200747.summary: The Kai Ken comes from the mountain-ringed Kai district of Japan, where it was used for deer and boar. A compact, well-muscled body, erect ears and curled tail place it among Japanese spitz types, but the brindle coat gives it a sharply individual identity.
VBO:0200747.interestingFact: Kai tora-ken, an alternate name, evokes the tiger-like striping of the brindle coat.

VBO:0200748.summary: Kaikadi is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200749.summary: Kangal Dog is a large Turkish livestock guardian developed for protecting sheep across open country and harsh seasonal weather. Its short, dense coat, powerful rectangular frame, and dark facial mask are central to the breed’s look. Present-day work keeps it firmly tied to Turkish pastoral life.

VBO:0200751.summary: The Kanni is a lean southern Indian hound whose long legs, deep chest and tucked abdomen fit a fast visual hunter. Its breeding tract lies in Tamil Nadu’s Virudhunagar, Tuticorin and Tirunelveli districts; observed coats include black-and-tan, tan, cream and fawn.
VBO:0200751.interestingFact: A morphometric study documented regional variation rather than one universally fixed coat color.
VBO:0200751.historicalRoots: Tamil Nadu indigenous hound associated with hunting and companionship.

VBO:0200753.summary: Karakachan Dog is a dog breed or regional type associated with Greece.

VBO:0200754.summary: The Karelian Bear Dog is a black-and-white Nordic hunting spitz bred to hold elk or bear at bay with its bark. Sturdy rather than oversized, it has an erect-eared, dense-coated outline suited to northern forests and the stamina to keep large game in place for the hunter.
VBO:0200754.interestingFact: The breed was formalized in 1945, with its first dogs registered the following year.
VBO:0200754.historicalRoots: Karelian and Finnish big-game hunting spitz.

VBO:0200755.summary: Karelian Bear Laika is a dog breed or regional type associated with Finland.

VBO:0200758.summary: Karst Shepherd Dog is a Slovenian mountain guardian with an iron-gray, abundant coat and a robust but medium-sized frame. Written mention of the type appears in the late seventeenth century, while its traditional work centered on flocks in the Karst region. Its hanging ears and tail set it apart from erect-eared spitz herders.
VBO:0200758.interestingFact: Baron Janez Vajkart Valvasor mentioned the breed in a book published in 1689.
VBO:0200758.historicalRoots: Slovenian Karst flock and property guardian.

VBO:0200759.summary: The Keeshond is a Dutch spitz once familiar on canal barges as a watchful companion. Its stand-off gray-and-black double coat, curled plume and dark facial “spectacles” give it one of the most recognizable expressions among northern dogs.
VBO:0200759.interestingFact: The breed became a symbol of the Dutch Patriot movement, with its name linked to the leader Kees.
VBO:0200759.historicalRoots: Dutch barge companion and watchdog with spitz ancestry.

VBO:0200764.summary: The Kerry Blue Terrier is an Irish farm and sporting terrier whose soft, wavy coat matures into shades of slate blue. It once tackled vermin, badger and even otter; the clipped show outline is only one expression of a robust, long-legged working dog.
VBO:0200764.interestingFact: Kerry Blue puppies are born black; the blue coloring develops as the coat matures.
VBO:0200764.historicalRoots: Irish all-round farm and sporting terrier.

VBO:0200772.summary: Kintamani-Bali Dog is a native Indonesian spitz-type dog from the Kintamani highlands of Bali. A wedge head, pricked ears, sickle tail, and thick double coat form its mountain profile. Kept as a household companion around Sukawana, it comes from a region of volcanic slopes and forest.

VBO:0200774.summary: The Kishu Ken is a Japanese mountain hunting dog from the Kishu region, especially associated with wild boar. Its medium spitz frame, upright ears and curled or sickle tail suit a nimble hunter; today’s solid-colored coats followed an earlier period with more visible markings.
VBO:0200774.interestingFact: Japan designated the breed a natural monument in 1934, the year solid colors became the accepted standard.
VBO:0200774.historicalRoots: Kishu mountain hunter used mainly for wild boar.

VBO:0200778.summary: The Kombai comes from the Theni district of Tamil Nadu, with a name tied to Kombai village. It is a medium-sized, strong-bodied dog, usually light brown to tan, with a history of guarding farms and households in the region.

VBO:0200779.summary: Komondor is a large Hungarian livestock guardian with a dense, corded white coat that can make its powerful frame almost disappear. Its roots are tied to pastoral life in the Carpathian Basin, where sheep and other stock needed protection. The cords are a defining working feature and develop as the coat matures, rather than being a decorative trim.
VBO:0200779.interestingFact: The Komondor’s ancestors are associated with Magyar pastoral movements into the Carpathian Basin.

VBO:0200786.summary: The Kromfohrländer is a relatively recent German companion breed named for the Krom Fohr district near Siegen. Developed from wire-haired Fox Terrier and Grand Griffon Vendéen ancestry, it comes in rough and smooth coats, typically white with brown patches.
VBO:0200786.interestingFact: International recognition arrived in 1955, only a short time after the breed’s founding.
VBO:0200786.historicalRoots: German companion breed developed near Siegen in the mid-twentieth century.

VBO:0200793.summary: The Kuvasz is a large white Hungarian flock guardian with a strong frame and a dense, gently waved coat. Its roots reach the Carpathian basin, where protecting stock against predators shaped a dog able to watch open country without needing to herd the animals itself.
VBO:0200793.interestingFact: The breed also appears in Hungarian hunting history during the reign of King Matthias Corvinus.

VBO:0200800.summary: The Labrador Retriever began with working water dogs from Newfoundland and was refined as a retriever in Great Britain. Its broad head, strong tail, and weather-resistant coat still advertise that aquatic past.
VBO:0200800.interestingFact: The “otter tail” in breed descriptions is not just decorative: its thick, rounded shape is part of the Labrador’s water-working design.
VBO:0200800.historicalRoots: Newfoundland water-dog roots; developed as a retriever in Great Britain.

VBO:0200808.summary: Lancashire Heeler is a short-legged, sturdy English cattle dog from the Ormskirk area, also historically used for rabbiting and ratting. Its compact frame, prick ears, and close black-and-tan or liver-and-tan coat carry a small dog’s version of working-cattle toughness. Its precise ancestry remains uncertain.
VBO:0200808.interestingFact: Its proposed ancestry includes Welsh cattle dogs and Manchester Terriers, though the exact history remains unproven.
VBO:0200808.historicalRoots: Lancashire cattle and farm vermin work.

VBO:0200814.summary: The Lapponian Herder is a Finnish reindeer worker from the long Sámi pastoral tradition. Its close-fitting double coat, upright ears and long, low-carried tail distinguish this steady trotter from the more profusely coated Finnish Lapphund.
VBO:0200814.interestingFact: The two modern Lapponian breeds were separated in Finnish registry practice in 1966.
VBO:0200814.historicalRoots: Sámi reindeer-herding dog of northern Finland.

VBO:0200816.summary: The Large Münsterländer is a black-and-white German pointing dog with feathering and an athletic, balanced frame. Bred as a versatile gundog, it searches field, forest and water and retrieves after the shot; its color history is intertwined with the German longhaired pointing-dog family.
VBO:0200816.interestingFact: Its distinct breeding line grew after black-and-white dogs were excluded from the German Longhaired Pointer club.
VBO:0200816.historicalRoots: German versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

VBO:0200819.summary: Leonberger is a giant German companion and watch dog developed near Stuttgart in the nineteenth century. Breeder Heinrich Essig used large breeds including Newfoundland, Saint Bernard-type, and Pyrenean Mountain Dog stock while seeking a lion-like presence. Beneath its heavy mane and feathering is a balanced, muscular dog meant to move freely.
VBO:0200819.interestingFact: The lion in Leonberg’s town crest helped inspire Essig’s desired appearance.
VBO:0200819.historicalRoots: Nineteenth-century German giant companion and watchdog.

VBO:0200824.summary: The Lhasa Apso comes from high-altitude Tibet, where a small dog needed a dense, hard coat against wind, dust and cold. Its long hair and fall over the eyes are functional as well as striking; Britain first received examples in the early 1920s.
VBO:0200824.interestingFact: Early British fanciers grouped it with other shaggy Tibetan dogs under the loose name “Lhasa Terrier.”
VBO:0200824.historicalRoots: Tibetan highland companion; introduced to Britain in the 1920s.

VBO:0200836.summary: The Löwchen is a small French companion whose traditional lion trim turns a long, flowing coat into a dramatic silhouette. The haircut is old rather than a modern novelty: little lion dogs appear in European carving, tapestries and paintings across several centuries.

VBO:0200856.summary: Maltese is a tiny Mediterranean companion with a long, straight white coat that falls close to the ground. Small dogs of its type were kept around maritime settlements, and the exact origin behind the name remains uncertain. A long body and light, elegant carriage sit under the striking sheet of hair.
VBO:0200856.interestingFact: “Maltese” may draw on an old Semitic word associated with harbors, so the name does not establish a single island birthplace.

VBO:0200862.summary: The Manchester Terrier is a sleek black-and-tan English ratter whose name points to the city where it became a recognized show type. Its narrow head, close coat and swift outline recall nineteenth-century vermin control rather than a purely decorative terrier.
VBO:0200862.interestingFact: Manchester pub shows in the mid-1800s helped the terrier gain classes of its own.

VBO:0200865.summary: The Maremma Sheepdog is a large white Italian flock guardian from a tradition linking the Tuscan Maremma with Abruzzo's sheep country. Seasonal movement of flocks helped bring those regional dogs together; the thick pale coat and substantial body remain part of a working landscape.
VBO:0200865.interestingFact: Transhumance—the seasonal movement of livestock—helped join the Abruzzo and Maremma dogs into the modern breed.
VBO:0200865.historicalRoots: Italian Abruzzo and Maremma flock-protection dog.

VBO:0200867.summary: Mastiff is a giant British guard dog with a broad, deep body and a massive square-looking head. Mastiff-type dogs were known in Britain for centuries, including before the fifteenth-century Battle of Agincourt. Its short coat and dark mask leave the powerful architectural shape in full view.

VBO:0200893.summary: The Miniature Pinscher is a small German pinscher with a compact square frame, smooth coat and brisk, ground-covering trot. Although its outline can suggest a tiny Doberman, the breed has its own pinscher history and was already numerous in German studbooks by the early twentieth century.
VBO:0200893.interestingFact: The 1925 German studbook recorded more than 1,300 Miniature Pinschers.

VBO:0200896.summary: The Miniature Schnauzer condenses the German Schnauzer look into a small, sturdy square body. Harsh coat, strong brows and a bristling beard give it a serious expression; the breed arose around Frankfurt from smaller rough-haired pinscher stock at the turn of the twentieth century.
VBO:0200896.interestingFact: Early breeders worked through varied coat textures to establish the familiar wiry miniature Schnauzer outline.

Its solid, agile body served hunting in mountainous country, and the old name “black hound” reflects its most immediate visual feature. A written standard for the breed appeared in 1924.

VBO:0200919.summary: The Mucuchies is a large, mountain-built Venezuelan dog associated with the high Andes around Mérida. Its mostly white coat and sturdy guardian outline suit a breed remembered alongside farms, flocks, and national history. Because populations have been limited, modern preservation is an important part of the story.
VBO:0200919.interestingFact: Nevado, a dog traditionally described as a Mucuchies, became famous as a companion of Simón Bolívar and appears in the breed’s national folklore.
VBO:0200919.historicalRoots: Venezuelan Andean farm and livestock-guardian dog.

VBO:0200920.summary: The Mudhol Hound is a lean Indian sighthound associated with northern Karnataka and the western Deccan. Its long, narrow head, deep chest and strongly tucked abdomen suit swift pursuit across open country, while local breeders preserve both smooth and silky-coated forms.
VBO:0200920.interestingFact: University researchers measured 150 Mudhol Hounds in Bagalkot-area villages to document the regional type.
VBO:0200920.historicalRoots: Karnataka sighthound of the western Deccan.

VBO:0200921.summary: The Mudi is a nimble Hungarian herding dog with pricked ears, a wedge head and a wavy coat over the body. Developed from regional stock in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, it was used on demanding livestock as well as in farmyard watch work.
VBO:0200921.interestingFact: Its coat changes texture across the dog: the head and fronts of the legs are short-haired while the body is waved or lightly curled.
VBO:0200921.historicalRoots: Hungarian herding dog from local and prick-eared German stock.

VBO:0200930.summary: Neapolitan Mastiff is a massive Italian guard dog with a long, heavy body, deep folds, and a broad head. The breed survived around Naples and the foothills of Vesuvius for centuries. Its short coat and loose skin make the powerful southern Italian outline immediately recognizable.

VBO:0200932.summary: The Nederlandse Kooikerhondje is a small Dutch decoy dog with orange-red patches, feathered ears and a waving white-plumed tail. Working among reed screens, it draws curious ducks down a decoy pipe rather than retrieving them; the modern breed was rebuilt during World War II.
VBO:0200932.interestingFact: A Friesland farm bitch named Tommy became the foundation dog in Baroness van Hardenbroek’s revival.
VBO:0200932.historicalRoots: Dutch duck-decoy worker revived in the 1940s.

VBO:0200933.summary: Nenets Herding Laika is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200934.summary: The New Guinea Singing Dog is a small, agile canine lineage known for flexible movement, a wedge-shaped head, and extraordinary vocalizations. Its relationship to free-ranging New Guinea dogs and long-managed captive populations makes the story more complicated than a conventional modern breed.
VBO:0200934.interestingFact: Its famous call rises and shifts in pitch in a way listeners often compare to singing, and groups can blend their voices into striking choruses.
VBO:0200934.historicalRoots: New Guinea free-ranging dog lineage represented by both wild-associated and captive populations.

VBO:0200935.summary: The New Zealand Heading Dog is an upright, long-legged sheep worker descended from Border Collie stock. It casts around a flock and holds animals with eye and position rather than the Huntaway's voice; a short coat and quick reactions suit close work on large hill farms.
VBO:0200935.interestingFact: Handlers usually discourage barking in a heading dog, while they deliberately select for a deep bark in Huntaways.
VBO:0200935.historicalRoots: New Zealand sheep-heading dog developed from Border Collies.

VBO:0200937.summary: New Zealand Sheepdog is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200938.summary: The Newfoundland is a giant Canadian water dog with a massive frame, webbed feet, and a dense coat made for cold, wet work. Its history includes hauling, retrieving, and dramatic water rescues.
VBO:0200938.interestingFact: A Newfoundland’s swimming style uses a powerful down-and-out stroke that can look more like a breaststroke than the usual dog paddle.
VBO:0200938.historicalRoots: Canadian working water dog associated with Newfoundland fisheries and rescue work.

VBO:0200945.summary: Norfolk Terrier is a tiny, sturdy terrier from the farm-dog traditions of East Anglia. It shares early roots with the Norwich Terrier but keeps its own silhouette through small folded ears. Low legs, a short back, and a harsh coat give this little dog the compact working form expected of a vermin hunter.
VBO:0200945.historicalRoots: East Anglian farm and vermin terrier.

VBO:0200953.summary: The Norwegian Buhund is a square-built farm spitz with upright ears, a curled tail and a dense coat. Norway’s farmers used it for both herding and watch work, and the breed type appears in accounts reaching back toward the Viking Age.
VBO:0200953.interestingFact: The Norwegian word buhund means “farmstead dog.”
VBO:0200953.historicalRoots: Norwegian farm, herding and watch dog with old spitz roots.

VBO:0200954.summary: Norwegian Dunker Hound is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200955.summary: The Norwegian Elkhound is a compact gray Nordic hunting dog with a thick weatherproof coat, upright ears and a tightly curled tail. Traditionally it tracked moose through rough terrain, then held the animal's attention with barking and agile movement until the hunter caught up.

VBO:0200962.summary: Norwich Terrier is one of the smallest working terriers, a low, compact dog with upright ears and a wiry weatherproof coat. It emerged from the same East Anglian farm-dog background as the Norfolk Terrier, then became a distinct named breed. A short back and sturdy bone keep the lively outline grounded in practical vermin work.
VBO:0200962.historicalRoots: East Anglian farm and vermin terrier.

VBO:0200964.summary: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever was developed on Canada’s Atlantic coast to lure waterfowl toward hunters and then retrieve them. Smaller than many retrievers, it has an alert red-orange coat, feathered tail and energetic shoreline working style.
VBO:0200964.interestingFact: “Tolling” names the lure phase of the hunt, before the dog retrieves the downed birds.
VBO:0200964.historicalRoots: Nova Scotian waterfowl tolling and retrieving dog of the nineteenth century.

VBO:0200965.summary: Old Croatian Sighthound is a historical dog breed or type.

VBO:0200967.summary: Old English Bulldog is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0200969.summary: Old English Sheepdog is a square, heavily coated British sheepdog whose gray-and-white jacket and rolling gait are hard to mistake. Beneath the weather-resistant coat is an able-bodied country worker with a topline that rises gently toward the rear. It has long carried the nickname “Bob-Tail.”
VBO:0200969.interestingFact: Possible ancestors include European shepherd dogs mixed with British sheepdogs, though the exact lineage remains uncertain.
VBO:0200969.historicalRoots: British country sheepdog with mixed historical roots.

VBO:0200980.summary: The Otterhound is a large British scent hound built for following otter scent over land and through water. Its rough, oily coat, broad feet and resonant bay speak to that demanding former work; otter hunting is now banned in Britain.
VBO:0200980.interestingFact: Houndsmen called a land scent trail a “drag” and a waterborne one a “wash.”
VBO:0200980.historicalRoots: British otter-trailing scent hound, a former hunting role.

VBO:0200989.summary: The Patagonian Sheepdog is a Chilean worker from the southern sheep country, shaped by geographic isolation and generations of herding selection. Its medium frame, long or semi-long coat and often partly folded ears suit the rough climate of Aysén and Magallanes.

VBO:0200994.summary: Pekingese is a small Chinese companion with a broad head, flattened face, and lion-like coat around a low, compact body. Its heavy front end and flowing hair create a recognizable silhouette. The breed’s form still depends on free movement, clear breathing, and a coat that leaves the body’s shape visible.

VBO:0200995.summary: The Pembroke Welsh Corgi is a low, sturdy Welsh cattle dog with a foxlike head, upright ears and a surprising amount of working stamina in a small frame. Its shorter tail tradition and lighter outline help distinguish it from the longer, brush-tailed Cardigan.
VBO:0200995.interestingFact: The standard permits a natural short tail; tail length alone cannot identify every Pembroke.
VBO:0200995.historicalRoots: Welsh cattle herder with a compact low build.

VBO:0201004.summary: The Peruvian Hairless Dog is an ancient Peruvian companion with a sleek, spare silhouette and skin that makes every line visible. Hairless and coated dogs can both occur, and the breed comes in more than one size. Archaeological images show similarly hairless dogs long before the modern standard gave them a formal frame.
VBO:0201004.interestingFact: Pre-Columbian ceramics from several Peruvian cultures depict hairless dogs, giving the type an unusually visible archaeological trail.
VBO:0201004.historicalRoots: Ancient Peruvian hairless-dog tradition documented in pre-Columbian art.

VBO:0201016.summary: The Pharaoh Hound is Malta’s fine-lined rabbit hunter, moving with both sight and scent and listening closely when quarry is near. Its lean russet coat, large upright ears and flesh-colored nose make a clear Mediterranean silhouette.

VBO:0201017.summary: Phu Quoc Ridgeback is a dog breed or regional type associated with Vietnam.

VBO:0201029.summary: Pointer is a British gun dog built to find game and mark its location with a still, directed stance. A strong yet supple body, deep chest, and clean, flowing curves give the breed both endurance and speed. Its short coat leaves the outline easy to read: this is a field athlete whose shape follows the work of scenting and pointing.

VBO:0201032.summary: The Polish Greyhound, or Chart Polski, is a powerful Polish sighthound recorded in hunting art and writing from the thirteenth century onward. Its deep chest, strong limbs and more substantial build than many sighthounds match a history of open-country pursuit.
VBO:0201032.interestingFact: The FCI rejects a once-repeated theory that it originated from Greyhound–Borzoi crosses; the chronology does not fit.
VBO:0201032.historicalRoots: Polish hunting sighthound documented since the medieval period.

VBO:0201035.summary: The Polish Lowland Sheepdog is a compact, muscular herder wrapped in a long, thick coat. A little longer than tall, it historically moved sheep and watched property; the heavy fringe may hide its eyes, but the dog beneath is a sturdy all-weather worker.
VBO:0201035.interestingFact: The breed is often known by the initials PON, from its Polish name Polski Owczarek Nizinny.
VBO:0201035.historicalRoots: Polish lowland herding and farm-watch dog.

VBO:0201043.summary: Pomeranian is the toy-sized German Spitz, carrying pointed ears, a foxlike head, an ample ruff, and a plume tail over the back in a very small frame. A dense undercoat holds the outer hair away from the body. The shared Spitz heritage is visible in every part of its crisp, alert outline.

VBO:0201048.interestingFact: The French name caniche is linked to cane, the word for a female duck.
VBO:0201048.historicalRoots: French waterfowl dog of Barbet-related ancestry, later a companion in four sizes.

VBO:0201064.summary: The Porcelaine is a refined French scent hound with a gleaming white coat, orange patches and finely shaped head. Bred to drive small game toward waiting guns, it combines a light, elegant appearance with the sturdy legs and nose expected of a working pack hound.

VBO:0201067.summary: Portuguese Podengo spans three sizes and both smooth and wire coats. Upright ears, a wedge-like head, and a sickle tail tie the varieties together, while different sizes traditionally pursued different game in Portugal’s varied terrain. Large, medium, and small dogs each preserve a distinct version of the same hunting heritage.
VBO:0201067.historicalRoots: Portuguese warren and other hunting traditions.

VBO:0201071.summary: The Portuguese Sheepdog, or Cão da Serra de Aires, worked the Alentejo plains moving and watching sheep, cattle, goats, horses and pigs. Its long, shaggy coat and hardy, medium-sized frame suit a dog selected for distance and sharp changes in temperature.
VBO:0201071.interestingFact: The standard names five kinds of livestock in its traditional working brief.
VBO:0201071.historicalRoots: Alentejo all-purpose livestock herder and watcher.

VBO:0201077.summary: The Portuguese Water Dog worked along Portugal's coast, assisting fishing crews and retrieving from the water. Strong shoulders, a muscular body and either wavy or curly coat fit that swimming life; the Algarve became a center for the breed as fishing practices changed elsewhere.

VBO:0201087.summary: Pudelpointer is a German rough-coated pointing dog founded from Poodle and Pointer stock, then developed as a distinct versatile gundog. Its sturdy, slightly long body and coarse protective jacket suit field, woodland, and water work. A beard and eyebrows frame a head built for nose-led hunting.
VBO:0201087.interestingFact: The Poodle was used to create the foundation stock, but the breed was subsequently maintained apart from other pointing breeds.
VBO:0201087.historicalRoots: German versatile gundog from Poodle and Pointer stock.

VBO:0201088.summary: Puerto Rican Mastiff is a dog breed or regional type associated with Puerto Rico.

VBO:0201089.summary: The Pug has Chinese roots and a long history as a compact companion, later reaching Europe through Dutch trading networks. Its square body, curled tail, short coat and dark mask make a distinctive outline, with open nostrils and non-protruding eyes part of its functional form.
VBO:0201089.interestingFact: The FCI says open nostrils and eyes that do not protrude are part of correct breed type.

VBO:0201102.summary: The Puli is a compact Hungarian herding dog whose dense coat can form long cords, turning motion into a spectacular swish of texture. Underneath is a nimble, square-built worker rather than a walking mop. The cords are a coat structure, not a costume, and maintaining them is a serious piece of grooming craft.
VBO:0201102.interestingFact: A mature corded coat forms as the soft undercoat and coarser outer coat intertwine; owners separate the cords by hand rather than brushing them flat.
VBO:0201102.historicalRoots: Hungarian herding dog used around sheep.

VBO:0201105.summary: The Pumi is a Hungarian herder with a curly coat, narrow muzzle and ears that stand up before tipping forward. It took shape from Puli-type dogs crossed with prick-eared continental terrier types, producing a springy, alert farm worker suited even to larger stock.
VBO:0201105.interestingFact: It was recognized as a separate breed in the early twentieth century after long sharing roots with the Puli.
VBO:0201105.historicalRoots: Hungarian herder shaped from Puli and continental terrier types.

Its compact, muscular body and heavy coat suit the cold conditions of the northern peninsula. The breed also serves as a national symbol in the DPRK.

VBO:0201122.summary: The Rajapalayam is a medium dog from southern Tamil Nadu, with a compact body, white coat and tucked abdomen. Dropped ears, pale pink nose and eyelids, golden eyes and a gently curved tail give it a distinctive look around its namesake town.
VBO:0201122.interestingFact: The Rajapalayam takes its name from a town in Virudhunagar district, where local dogs have traditionally guarded farms and farmhouses.
VBO:0201122.historicalRoots: Rajapalayam district, Tamil Nadu indigenous working dog.

VBO:0201123.summary: Rampur Greyhound is a dog breed or regional type associated with India.

VBO:0201125.summary: Rat Terrier is an American farm terrier bred for controlling rats and other small vermin. Its smooth coat, sharply alert ears, and compact but athletic body suit quick turns in barns and fields. The breed comes in miniature and standard sizes, with a practical working outline that remains recognizable across both.

VBO:0201132.summary: The Redbone Coonhound is an American scent hound bred to trail and tree raccoons. It carries a smooth, rich red coat, long ears and an athletic outline; selective breeding gradually replaced the black saddle markings seen on many early dogs.
VBO:0201132.interestingFact: George F. L. Birdsong’s Georgia hounds were important foundation stock for the modern breed.
VBO:0201132.historicalRoots: U.S. raccoon-trailing and treeing hound with Georgia foundation lines.

VBO:0201134.summary: Retriever is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0201135.summary: The Rhodesian Ridgeback is a large southern African hound with one unmistakable signature: a narrow ridge of hair running forward along the back. Developed from European dogs and ridged local dogs, it was used for varied farm and hunting work.
VBO:0201135.interestingFact: The ridge is made by hair growing in the opposite direction from the rest of the coat and is defined by a pair of symmetrical crowns near the shoulders.
VBO:0201135.historicalRoots: Southern African multipurpose hound developed from imported and local ridged dogs.

VBO:0201137.summary: The Romagna Water Dog began as a curly-coated retriever in the marshes around Ravenna and Comacchio. When those wetlands were drained, its exceptional nose found a new purpose in truffle searching; the compact square body and dense woolly curls still echo its water-dog past.
VBO:0201137.interestingFact: Few breeds have such a clear job change: from retrieving in marsh water to finding truffles in the hills.
VBO:0201137.historicalRoots: Romagna marsh retriever turned truffle-searching dog.

VBO:0201141.summary: Romanian Mioritic Shepherd Dog comes from the Carpathians, where large dogs were selected for flock work and guarding. A long, abundant coat covers the head, body, and legs, giving a sweeping outline to a strong, mobile dog. Males are typically taller and more powerful than females, with a clear difference in build.

VBO:0201143.interestingFact: The old “Rottweil butcher’s dog” could guard cattle and property and also pull loads.

VBO:0201160.interestingFact: The hospice's dogs appear in records from the 1600s and became renowned for rescue work in the mountain pass.

VBO:0201171.summary: The Saluki is a tall Middle Eastern sighthound whose long history is written in a light frame, deep chest, and effortless-looking stride. Both feathered and smooth coats occur. Across a vast region, related local types were valued for hunting by sight, so the breed’s story is broader than any single country or coat color.
VBO:0201171.interestingFact: The familiar feathered ears are only one expression of the breed: smooth Salukis carry the same elegant structure without the long furnishings.
VBO:0201171.historicalRoots: Ancient Middle Eastern sighthound tradition spanning multiple regions and local types.

VBO:0201174.summary: Samoyed is a white Arctic spitz with an upcurved mouth, dark eyes, and a thick coat that forms the famous “Samoyed smile.” Dogs associated with northern Russian and Siberian peoples worked in reindeer herding, hunting, and sledding, often living close to their families. Beneath the bright coat is a medium-sized, endurance-oriented working shape.
VBO:0201174.interestingFact: Northern Samoyed dogs lived so close to their people that they sometimes slept inside shelters for warmth.
VBO:0201174.historicalRoots: Northern Russian and Siberian sled and reindeer work.

VBO:0201180.summary: The Šarplaninac is a mountain livestock guardian associated with the Šar range of the Balkans. A long, coarse coat, substantial bone and steady, ground-covering frame suit long outdoor watches over cattle herds rather than fast pursuit.
VBO:0201180.interestingFact: The FCI standard lists both North Macedonia and Serbia in the breed’s official origin.
VBO:0201180.historicalRoots: Balkan livestock guardian of the Šar mountain region.

VBO:0201181.summary: The Schapendoes is a light Dutch sheepdog under a profuse, slightly wavy coat, with a shaggy face and long feathered tail. Heathland shepherds valued its speed, endurance and jumping ability when flocks ranged far from villages; the floating outline hides a nimble worker.
VBO:0201181.interestingFact: The breed nearly vanished as Dutch sheep flocks declined, then was rebuilt by enthusiasts in the twentieth century.

VBO:0201182.summary: Schiller Hound is a dog breed or regional type associated with Sweden.

VBO:0201184.summary: Schipperke is a small Belgian sheepdog-type companion and watcher with a wedge head, erect ears, and an all-black coat that rises into a dramatic neck ruff. It was already familiar in Flemish working neighborhoods in the seventeenth century. Strong, square, and fine-boned at once, it packs an unmistakable outline into a compact body.
VBO:0201184.interestingFact: “Schipperke” comes from a Flemish expression meaning “little shepherd.”

VBO:0201185.summary: The Schnauzer is the medium-sized German stable dog once called a rough-haired Pinscher. Its square body, wiry coat, strong eyebrows and beard give the familiar outline; horses and a knack for catching rodents shaped its early farmyard role.
VBO:0201185.interestingFact: The breed was known as a “Rattler” before the Schnauzer name took hold.
VBO:0201185.historicalRoots: Southern German stable and rodent-control dog.

VBO:0201195.summary: The Scottish Deerhound is a giant rough-coated sighthound shaped to chase red deer across Scottish open country. Its long legs, deep chest and wiry cloak give the impression of a larger, shaggy Greyhound, but the scale reflects a quarry that demanded speed, strength and endurance together.

VBO:0201198.summary: Scottish Terrier is a low, long-headed Highland terrier with short legs, a hard coat, and a powerful rear. The dark, sculptural profile has become famous, but the underlying breed was shaped as a tough ground-working terrier. A pronounced beard and eyebrows frame the head without changing its strong, narrow form.
VBO:0201198.interestingFact: The Scottish Terrier Club formed in 1882, shortly after the first breed standard.

VBO:0201199.summary: Sealydale Terrier is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0201200.summary: The Sealyham Terrier is a small but substantial Welsh working terrier, longer than it is tall, with a weather-resistant white coat and strong jaws. Its compact build recalls earth work even though the modern dog is often encountered as a companion.
VBO:0201200.interestingFact: The official outline is oblong rather than square, despite its short legs.
VBO:0201200.historicalRoots: Welsh earth-working terrier later kept as a companion.

VBO:0201207.summary: The Serbian Hound is a medium Balkan scent hound in warm red tones with a black saddle across the back. Built with strong legs and close coat for long tracking days, it preserves a regional hunting tradition once cataloged under the broader name Balkan Hound.
VBO:0201207.interestingFact: The name changed from Balkan Hound to Serbian Hound to reflect where the breed was most established.

VBO:0201217.summary: Shetland Sheepdog is a small, long-coated sheepdog named for Scotland’s Shetland Islands. A refined wedge head, abundant mane, and agile movement give it a light working silhouette. Its dual history as sheepdog and companion is visible in a balanced frame under the profuse coat.
VBO:0201217.interestingFact: Its coat includes a dense undercoat beneath long, straight outer hair.

VBO:0201218.summary: Shi-Jug is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0201220.summary: The Shiba Inu is the smallest of Japan’s native spitz breeds, with a compact frame, curled tail, and an expression that can move from solemn to mischievous in a heartbeat. It was historically used for hunting in mountainous terrain.
VBO:0201220.interestingFact: The origin of “Shiba” is debated: it may refer to brushwood, an old regional word for small, or the reddish color of autumn brush.
VBO:0201220.historicalRoots: Japanese native hunting spitz associated with mountainous regions.

VBO:0201222.summary: Shichon is a named crossbreed. Dogs of this cross can vary widely in appearance and size, including within the same litter.

VBO:0201223.summary: The Shih Tzu’s roots lie in Tibet, but the breed developed in Chinese imperial palaces before reaching Britain in the 1930s. A long coat and hair rising over the nose create its distinctive “chrysanthemum” face on a sturdy small companion.
VBO:0201223.interestingFact: Britain first recorded imports in 1931 and gave the Shih Tzu a separate register in 1940.
VBO:0201223.historicalRoots: Tibetan roots and Chinese palace development as a companion dog.

VBO:0201225.summary: The Shikoku is a medium Japanese mountain dog developed for wild boar hunting in Kochi Prefecture. Pricked ears, a tightly carried tail and sesame coat mark its spitz silhouette, while the compact, strong body suited steep, difficult terrain.
VBO:0201225.interestingFact: Its older local strains carried the names Awa, Hongawa and Hata, each tied to a breeding area.

VBO:0201233.summary: Siberian Husky is a medium northern sled dog built to carry light loads at moderate speed over great distances. A moderately compact frame, dense double coat, erect ears, and brush tail balance strength with quick, economical movement. It moves smoothly in harness and carries a lighter frame than many Arctic freight dogs.

VBO:0201237.summary: The Silky Terrier is an Australian toy terrier developed from Australian and Yorkshire terrier lines. Its small, sturdy frame carries a fine blue-and-tan coat that falls straight and glossy, combining a polished look with unmistakable terrier ancestry.
VBO:0201237.interestingFact: The first breed standard was drawn up in Australia in the early twentieth century.
VBO:0201237.historicalRoots: Australian companion terrier shaped from local and Yorkshire lines.

VBO:0201240.summary: The Skye Terrier is a long, low Scottish terrier whose straight fall of hair can nearly touch the ground. It came from the Western Isles working-terrier tradition; beneath the dramatic coat is a strong, short-legged dog, and both erect and dropped ears belong to the breed.
VBO:0201240.interestingFact: Greyfriars Bobby, a Skye Terrier remembered for his vigil by his owner’s Edinburgh grave, has a memorial near the churchyard.

VBO:0201242.summary: Sloughi is a North African sighthound with a spare, long-legged body and a fine, short coat. It has lived across the region for centuries and remains strongly associated with Morocco. Lean muscle and a deep chest give it an elegant but unmistakably athletic outline.

VBO:0201278.summary: The Spanish Mastiff traveled with Spain’s seasonal Merino sheep movements, protecting flocks from wolves and other predators. Its immense body, thick loose skin and dense coat suit an animal bred to stay with livestock across varied routes and pastures.
VBO:0201278.interestingFact: Its working history is tied to the medieval Mesta association of transhumant sheep breeders.
VBO:0201278.historicalRoots: Spanish transhumant flock guardian, especially with Merino sheep.

VBO:0201280.summary: The Spanish Water Dog is a rustic, curly-coated worker from Spain with a long résumé: herding, water work, and help around farms and fishing communities. Its coat can form cords when left to grow, giving the dog a graphic, woolly outline.
VBO:0201280.interestingFact: Traditional coat care avoids sculpting the curls into a showy shape—the coat is usually clipped to one even length and allowed to grow naturally.
VBO:0201280.historicalRoots: Spanish multipurpose working dog used for herding and water-related tasks.

VBO:0201309.summary: Sussex Spaniel is a low, substantial British flushing dog with a rich golden-liver coat and a distinctive rolling movement. It was built to push through thick cover at a steady pace and to give voice while working, a useful signal when a hunter could not see the dog. Its solemn expression masks a field shape with strength and persistence.

VBO:0201315.summary: The Swedish Lapphund is a dark-coated Nordic spitz long associated with the Sámi communities of northern Scandinavia. It served in reindeer herding, hunting and watch work; an upright-eared, curled-tailed silhouette remains central to its identity.
VBO:0201315.interestingFact: The FCI describes it today chiefly as a versatile companion, after centuries of northern working use.
VBO:0201315.historicalRoots: Sámi reindeer-herding, hunting and watch dog of Sweden.

VBO:0201316.summary: The Swedish Vallhund is a low, long-bodied Swedish farm spitz built to work around cattle. Short strong legs, erect ears and a dense sable coat with pale 'harness' markings make a memorable outline; the tail may take several natural forms.

Its proportions and coat suit coursing across broken upland terrain.

VBO:0201342.summary: The Tenterfield Terrier is a small Australian terrier with a smooth coat, alert ears and a balanced, athletic frame. Descended from working terriers brought by English settlers, it was valued on farms and around homesteads for controlling rats and other vermin.
VBO:0201342.interestingFact: A natural bobtail occurs in the breed; Dogs Australia describes it as a distinctive Tenterfield feature.
VBO:0201342.historicalRoots: Australian farm and homestead vermin-control terrier.

VBO:0201347.summary: The Thai Bangkaew Dog is a square-built spitz from Bangkaew village in Phitsanulok province. A dense stand-off coat, foxlike face and plumed tail give it a crisp outline; local breeding turned a village dog into a breed recognized across Thailand.
VBO:0201347.interestingFact: The FCI history connects the breed's name directly to Bangkaew village, its place of origin.

VBO:0201348.summary: The Thai Ridgeback is a lean, muscular dog from Thailand with a short coat and a ridge running against the grain along its back. Geographic isolation helped preserve a distinctive local type with upright ears and a clean, athletic silhouette. Modern dogs can vary, but the ridge remains the breed’s visual headline.
VBO:0201348.interestingFact: Only a small group of breeds carries a dorsal hair ridge; in the Thai Ridgeback, its shape can vary from a narrow needle to broader leaf-like patterns.
VBO:0201348.historicalRoots: Long-established Thai ridged dog associated with eastern regions of the country.

VBO:0201350.summary: Tibetan Kyi Apso is a dog breed or regional type associated with Tibet.

VBO:0201351.summary: Tibetan Mastiff, or Do Khyi, is a large Himalayan guardian historically associated with nomadic herders and Tibetan monasteries. Heavy bone, a broad head, and a dense coat with a neck mane give it a commanding mountain outline. Males may take at least four years to reach full maturity.

VBO:0201352.summary: The Tibetan Spaniel is a small, slightly long-bodied companion dog from Tibet. Its silky coat, plumed tail and alert expression give a compact but poised outline; despite the name, it belongs to the Tibetan companion-dog tradition rather than the field spaniels.
VBO:0201352.interestingFact: Its FCI classification is among Tibetan companion breeds, not hunting spaniels.

VBO:0201353.summary: The Tibetan Terrier is a shaggy, medium-sized Tibetan dog whose name is a historical misfit: it is not a true terrier. A sturdy square frame, long coat and broad feet served herding and travel with traders; it later became best known as a companion.
VBO:0201353.interestingFact: The feet are notably large, flat and round, giving a snowshoe-like spread over rough ground.
VBO:0201353.historicalRoots: Tibetan herding, travel and companion dog.

VBO:0201356.summary: Tornjak is a livestock guardian from the mountain districts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. Its nearly square, powerful body is covered by a long, thick coat, yet it remains an agile mover. Modern breeders rebuilt the breed from scattered surviving shepherd-dog stock after its numbers had become very low.
VBO:0201356.interestingFact: Historical documents dated 1067 and 1374 mention dogs associated with the Tornjak’s region.
VBO:0201356.historicalRoots: Bosnian and Croatian mountain livestock protection.

VBO:0201361.summary: The Toy Fox Terrier is a distinctly American miniature of the Smooth Fox Terrier tradition. A sleek, mostly white coat and lithe square body sit on toy scale, while its early usefulness as a barnyard ratter kept the breed’s working-terrier character visible.
VBO:0201361.interestingFact: AKC history records small Smooth Fox Terriers working on American farms before the breed was stabilized.
VBO:0201361.historicalRoots: American small farm ratter developed from Smooth Fox Terrier stock.

VBO:0201389.summary: Vizsla is Hungary’s short-haired pointing and retrieving dog, recognizable by a lean frame and uniform russet-gold coat. It works through fields, forests, and water, with a nose and gait suited to locating and recovering game. Its ancestors accompanied Magyar movements into the Carpathian Basin, and Hungarian hunting records reach back centuries.
VBO:0201389.interestingFact: Hungarian documents and illustrations depicting the type reach back to the fourteenth century.
VBO:0201389.historicalRoots: Hungarian versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

VBO:0201390.summary: The Volpino Italiano is a small Italian spitz with a dense stand-off coat, pointed ears and a plume curling over its back. Long kept by both wealthy households and ordinary workers, it served as a bright little watchdog as well as a companion.
VBO:0201390.interestingFact: The FCI history notes a Volpino in a Venetian painting by Vittore Carpaccio dated 1502.
VBO:0201390.historicalRoots: Italian household watchdog and companion with European spitz roots.

VBO:0201401.summary: The Weimaraner is a silver-gray German gundog built to work field, forest and water before and after the shot. Its long, clean lines and strong muscles suit that varied job; records connect the early breed to the Weimar court and later to professional hunters in central Germany.
VBO:0201401.interestingFact: Its pale gray coat gives it one of the most immediately recognizable silhouettes among continental pointers.
VBO:0201401.historicalRoots: German versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

VBO:0201411.summary: Welsh Springer Spaniel is a compact, enduring flushing dog with a vivid red-and-white coat. Its balanced, not overly leggy body was built for hard work through Welsh cover, with drive that shows in its brisk movement. Although related in purpose to other spaniels, the Welsh Springer keeps a distinct color and a longer, tapered head.

VBO:0201412.summary: The Welsh Terrier is a compact black-and-tan working terrier with a tight wiry coat. It was used in Wales to hunt fox, badger and otter, leaving a strong, practical outline beneath the tidy beard and lively expression.
VBO:0201412.interestingFact: The breed may share older Celtic roots with the similar-looking Lakeland Terrier, though the standard treats that link as a possibility.
VBO:0201412.historicalRoots: Welsh fox, badger and otter working terrier.

VBO:0201415.summary: The West Highland White Terrier is a compact Scottish earthdog in a crisp white double coat. Strong quarters and short legs made sense among moorland rocks; its Poltalloch roots link it with other west Highland terriers, while the white color became its defining visual signature.
VBO:0201415.interestingFact: Earlier names included Poltalloch Terrier and Roseneath Terrier.

VBO:0201419.summary: Wetterhoun is a Frisian water dog from the northern Netherlands, historically used for otter and other small-predator hunting and to watch the yard. Its square, sturdy body and tightly curled coat fit work around Friesland’s lakes and waterways. The breed’s history is local and practical, with cart-pulling also recorded in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
VBO:0201419.historicalRoots: Frisian water hunting and farmyard work.

VBO:0201421.summary: The Whippet is a medium British sighthound: all sweeping curves, tucked waist, and surprising acceleration. It became closely associated with working-class racing and rabbit coursing, earning the affectionate nickname “the poor man’s racehorse.” At rest the outline can look delicate; in motion it makes perfect mechanical sense.
VBO:0201421.interestingFact: Whippets were once raced down straight tracks toward a waving cloth, a working-class sport that helped shape both the breed and its enduring speed-dog image.
VBO:0201421.historicalRoots: British sighthound developed for racing and small-game coursing.

VBO:0201422.summary: White Shepherd is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0201423.summary: The White Swiss Shepherd Dog grew from white shepherd lines maintained in North America and then established in Switzerland from the 1970s. Its upright ears, white double coat and balanced herding-dog frame combine a familiar shepherd outline with a distinct Swiss breed history.
VBO:0201423.interestingFact: A male named Lobo, born in 1966, is cited as a progenitor of the Swiss population.
VBO:0201423.historicalRoots: North American white shepherd ancestry established as a Swiss breed.

VBO:0201424.summary: The Wire Fox Terrier is a compact British terrier with a short back, longish narrow head and sharply textured coat. Its forward-folding V ears and quick, tiptoe stance give a ready-to-go look; the wire coat is a defining contrast with the separate smooth-coated Fox Terrier.
VBO:0201424.interestingFact: The coat should be dense and harsh enough to give a crisp outline, with softer hair underneath.

VBO:0201425.summary: Wire Haired Whippet is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0201426.summary: Wire-Haired Jack Russell Terrier is a dog breed or regional type.

VBO:0201427.summary: Wirehaired Pointing Griffon is a rough-coated European gundog refined by Eduard Korthals in the nineteenth century. Its medium, slightly long body, square muzzle, beard, and eyebrows create a practical field silhouette. The versatile pointer can also follow the trail of wounded large game.

VBO:0201428.summary: The Wirehaired Vizsla is a Hungarian pointing dog created in the 1930s by crossing the shorthaired Vizsla with the German Wirehaired Pointer. It retained the field role and golden-rust coloring of the Vizsla while adding a harsh coat, brows and beard for a rougher outline.
VBO:0201428.interestingFact: The wire coat marks a comparatively recent branch of the older Hungarian Vizsla tradition.
VBO:0201428.historicalRoots: Hungarian versatile pointing dog created in the 1930s.

VBO:0201435.summary: The Xiasi Dog comes from Guizhou in southwestern China, where it is known for a compact, quick-moving body. Its usually white, harsh coat, bristly muzzle and upright triangular ears make a distinctive regional silhouette.
VBO:0201435.interestingFact: Stiff, needle-like guard hairs can stand up around the face and muzzle.

VBO:0201436.summary: The Xoloitzcuintli—usually shortened to Xolo—is an ancient Mexican breed with both hairless and coated varieties and three recognized sizes. The hairless form reveals every elegant angle, while the coated form is a reminder that the breed is more genetically and visually varied than its best-known image suggests.
VBO:0201436.interestingFact: Its name joins Xolotl, an Aztec deity, with itzcuintli, a Nahuatl word for dog; saying “Xolo” is the friendly shortcut.
VBO:0201436.historicalRoots: Ancient Mexican dog represented in pre-Columbian culture and modern hairless and coated forms.

VBO:0201442.interestingFact: Written references to dogs in the Yakutia region begin in the seventeenth century.

VBO:0201448.summary: The Yorkshire Terrier came from the same nineteenth-century English region as the much larger Airedale. Beneath its long blue-and-tan silk coat sits a small terrier once valued for pursuing rodents; the present breed name was accepted in 1870.
VBO:0201448.interestingFact: Its early ancestry included the old Black and Tan Terrier, with Maltese and Skye Terrier influence also noted by the FCI.
VBO:0201448.historicalRoots: Yorkshire terrier developed in the mid-nineteenth century from several small terrier lines.

VBO:0201454.summary: The German Pinscher is a medium, square-built German watchdog with a short, close coat and clean, athletic lines. It shares early ancestry with the Schnauzer; what separated the smooth-haired Pinscher was its coat, making a strikingly different silhouette from a related working stock.
VBO:0201454.interestingFact: Older records called the Schnauzer the rough-coated Pinscher, reflecting their shared roots.
VBO:0201454.historicalRoots: German smooth-coated watch and companion dog.

VBO:0201455.summary: The French Bulldog took shape in the working neighborhoods of Paris in the 1880s. Compact and muscular, with a short coat and upright bat ears, it moved from the circles of porters, butchers and coachmen into Parisian social and artistic life.
VBO:0201455.interestingFact: The first breed club was founded in Paris in 1880, with the first registration recorded in 1885.
VBO:0201455.historicalRoots: Parisian companion dog developed in the late nineteenth century.
